transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-04-21
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Blake (Redwood AE); Sofia Patel (Redwood SE); Marcus Lee (Redwood CSM); Elaine Rivers (VP Eng, Pioneer); Tomás Ortega (SRE); Priya Nair (Head of Platform); Aaron Chu (Infra)

Auto-generated Summary: quick follow-up after the cascade on 2026-04-14. Main ask: why did the fallback to smaller model variants not kick and why did the KV cache appear stale across regions.

Topics: incident timeline, shortfalls in playbooks, telemetry gaps, forensics retention needs, tabletop drill scheduling.

[00:00] Jordan (Redwood): hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. really appreciate you making time. the main goal here is to align on what happened during the 14th, and figure out concrete playbook changes. will start by walking through our timeline.
[00:28] Elaine (Pioneer): thanks Jordan. um, for context, this incident hit two of our regions, and the user-facing latency spiked for about 40 minutes. our customers flagged degraded responses and some repeated failures. we fell back to cached responses in some clients but others got timeouts.
[00:56] Sofia (Redwood): quick clarification - when you say 'cached responses', are those local browser caches or prefix caching at the Redwood layer?
[01:12] Tomás (Pioneer): it's a mix, some app-side caches and then Redwood's prefix cache. we noticed the K V cache didn't seem to have any hits for certain tenant prefixes. it showed up as 0% on a couple of shards.
[01:38] Jordan (Redwood): okay thanks. our initial root cause hypothesis was that an autoscaler oscillation plus a routing flapping caused sessions to lose their KV context so the smaller-context model got promoted prematurely and then failed fallback policies. but that's still tentative.
[02:08] Priya (Pioneer): just to add, we have strict data retention rules so we couldn't keep raw request payloads beyond 48 hours, which limited what we could share forensics-wise. that might be affecting post-incident analysis.
[02:34] Marcus (Redwood): noted - we'll flag retention as an action item. there might be ways to provide pseudonymized traces to you that respect your KMS constraints.

[03:05] Elaine: one big question from execs is why the automatic canary fallback to the smaller but more robust model didn't kick in - we expected the platform to route to model-var-B when model-var-A's latency crossed 500ms. instead requests errored.
[03:34] Sofia: yeah, looking at the logs the routing policy did initiate a variant switch but a subset of requests failed because the KV cache had stale slot keys so the decoder path couldn't resume the session. there was an error during KV retrieval that looked like a permission + timeout mix, weirdly.
[04:02] Tomás: permission? we didn't change IAM around there. could it be a transient KMS hiccup?
[04:16] Jordan: our trace shows a burst of KMS errors at 10:18:42 UTC originating from a single control plane instance that later restarted. that coincided with a spike in fan-out. the restart caused a short lived policy evaluation delay.
[04:44] Aaron (Pioneer): when you say policy evaluation delay, do you mean RBAC decision latency? we've seen that in our infra when the auth cache invalidates.
[04:58] Sofia: yes, RBAC + KMS handshake delay. logs show the control plane retried a number of times before it served a 403 for the KV read which propagated as a session loss.

[05:26] Elaine: okay, so there's a chain: control plane restart -> KMS/RBAC handshake delays -> KV reads fail -> model fallback doesn't have context -> requests error. is that the short chain?
[05:44] Jordan: that's the working chain, yes. but we need to verify across our replicas because we observed inconsistent behavior - some regions had successful fallbacks while others didn't.

[06:07] Priya: the inconsistent region behavior is a big concern. it suggests some of our routing/replication of prefix caches wasn't synchronous. our config uses eventual replication for performance, and during high QPS that probably created windows where new replicas had empty prefix entries.
[06:34] Tomás: exactly, so two factors: replication lag and the KMS permission transient. both amplified the failure mode.

[06:58] Marcus: let's capture that as a hypothesis: replication lag + auth/KMS transient cause KV miss, leading to failed fallback. next step is to validate with traces. Jordan, Sofia, can Redwood export the per-tenant KV access traces around the 10:18:00 to 10:22:00 UTC window?
[07:24] Sofia: yes we can. we'll need to pull KV access logs and control plane logs; there will be PII in some payloads so we have to scrub. we'll export hashes and timestamps.
[07:42] Elaine: also, we need to confirm retention. as Priya mentioned, our policy is 48 hours; if we want deeper forensics both sides will need to agree on temporary retention increases.

[08:05] Jordan: agreed. we'll propose a scoped retention extension for the tenant under stricter access controls; we can keep only the metadata + hashed prefixes for two weeks if that satisfies you.
[08:27] Priya: hashed prefixes and RBAC-limited storage sound workable. we'll confirm internally but it's positive.

[08:50] Tomás: beyond forensics, we need durable playbook changes. our ops folks reported the runbook attempted an automated restart but the playbook had ambiguous ownership between application SRE and the security team for KMS faults. that slowed remediation.
[09:16] Elaine: yes, the handoff was unclear. execs want an explicit sequence: who restarts control plane, who escalates KMS, who flips routing policy, etc.
[09:34] Marcus: we can help draft an explicit playbook that assigns owners for each fail state. we'll also include a checklist for the tabletop.

[09:58] Sofia: technical note - we should consider adding a synchronous prefix replication option for tenants with strict tail-latency requirements. it costs more but removes the replication window. we can expose that as a config flag or a dedicated plan.
[10:22] Priya: cost is a factor, but for certain high-value flows we can justify it. we'll need a quote on delta-cost and expected improvement in tail P95/P99.

[10:45] Jordan: also, a short term mitigation: increase the aggressiveness of the fallback policy to not require KV reads for the first N tokens after a variant switch - basically warm the model with a small stateless prompt until KV reads succeed. it's a tradeoff in coherence but reduces errors.
[11:10] Aaron: that might be acceptable for customer-facing search UX but not for highly stateful chat sessions. we need nuance by product.

[11:33] Elaine: can Redwood provide a matrix of fallback behaviors by product type? that will help our product teams decide acceptable coherence vs availability tradeoffs.
[11:48] Sofia: yes, we'll provide a matrix: full-state fallback, partial-state warm-start, stateless fallback, and the expected failure modes for each.

[12:02] Tomás: on alerts: our alerting thresholds didn't clearly map to the cascading failure. we got high CPU alerts but not composite errors that indicate KV/permission chains. we need better signal composition.
[12:25] Marcus: Redwood can push a recommended alert bundle that includes KMS error rates, prefix replication lag, failed KV reads, model variant error rates, and correlated spikes. we'll send the bundle as a terraform module or plain alert rules.

[12:48] Priya: great - 'terraform-able' alerts would be ideal. we can adopt them quickly.

[13:05] Elaine: security requirement - our compliance team needs proof of audit logs for the control plane actions during an incident. do you capture immutable audit logs and can you export them under SAML-based access?
[13:27] Jordan: yes, we maintain immutable audit logs. exports require elevated RBAC and we can provide SAML-based access to a read-only bucket; may need a short access agreement for the incident retention window.
[13:46] Priya: also, KMS access: we need to ensure Redwood's Temporary Access to decrypt traces is auditable and limited.
[14:02] Sofia: we already use a customer-controlled KMS flow in Private deploys; for hosted we do a wrapped-key approach. for the incident, we can request short-lived wrapped keys and record all decrypt operations in audit logs.

[14:28] Tomás: going back to runbooks - Priya, can you send the sections where the KMS handoff is described? that will help Redwood craft clearer owner transitions.
[14:42] Priya: yes, I'll extract those and highlight the ambiguous steps.

[15:00] Jordan: cool, let me outline proposed playbook changes: 1) explicit owner for KMS faults; 2) option to enable synchronous prefix replication; 3) a fallback policy matrix with warm-start options; 4) composite alert bundle; 5) a controlled retention window for forensics. we'll circulate a draft within 48 hours.
[15:26] Elaine: sounds good. timeline?
[15:31] Jordan: we'll share draft by 2026-04-23.

[15:38] Sofia: technical ask - we need to pull the per-shard KV hit/miss histogram for tenant foo-342 for the event window. that'll show which shards had replication lag.
[15:53] Tomás: I can create a temp account with read access to storage so Redwood can pull those histograms, if that's easiest.
[16:05] Aaron: before we give access, we need an SCIM entry and an access justification; we'll work with your security contact during export time.

[16:22] Jordan: noted - Marcus, can you coordinate the minimum scope and a pre-signed S3 read-only link model?
[16:31] Marcus: yep I'll own.

[16:36] Elaine: another operational gap - our runbooks don't define a good rollback safe state for rolling the control plane. some engineers restarted replicas, which later caused split-brain detection to slow things down. we need a clear safe-sequence.
[16:55] Sofia: Redwood can provide a rollback play sequence; but we'd like to run it in a tabletop first to validate assumptions.

[17:10] Priya: tabletop will be high priority. Marcus, please get invites out for the week of 2026-05-04. we'll include security, infra, and product.
[17:22] Marcus: will do.

[17:30] Tomás: small nit: the telemetry we saw lacked correlation IDs in some paths so linking user request to KV reads was manual. adding a request-level correlation id everywhere would speed triage.
[17:46] Sofia: that's a good call. we can add a correlation token to the front-end routing in the flow. might be a small perf cost but huge triage benefit.

[18:03] Elaine: okay, let's recap actions. Jordan to send incident timeline and draft playbook by 4/23. Sofia to export KV traces and histograms by 4/24. Priya to send runbook excerpts by 4/25. Marcus to schedule tabletop and circulate pre-read by 4/28. Tomás to surface alert thresholds and correlation id work.

[18:33] Jordan: any outstanding concerns?
[18:38] Aaron: one more - do you have a recommended SLA tweak or shield we could buy short-term for peak windows so we don't hit this again during launches?
[18:52] Jordan: we can offer a temporary dedicated replication lane for that tenant or an elevated plan with synchronous replication. we'll include cost delta in the playbook draft.

[19:09] Elaine: fine. execs will want the cost/benefit.
[19:14] Jordan: understood.

[19:25] Sofia: last technical note: we saw a peculiar 403 pattern from one control plane instance; our postmortem will include a heap/GC and network snapshot for that instance. it might reveal why the KMS handshake failed.
[19:44] Jordan: thanks. okay folks, we'll get the artifacts out. Marcus will coordinate tabletop invites.

[20:00] (wrap) Marcus: thanks everyone. we'll end there and follow up with calendar invites and the artifact bundle.

End of transcript.

Artifacts mentioned in chat: https://redwood.internal/incidents/2026-04-14-heap-osc ; https://redwood.internal/playbooks/pioneer-kv-fallback-draft-v1 ; KV histogram to be shared via pre-signed link.
